title: Raffle Stub Lookup
story: You run the raffle at a school fair. Every ticket you sold left a stub, and the stubs are filed in one long list from the lowest ticket number to the highest. Not every number was sold, so there are gaps.
The head teacher reads out a winning number. Before anyone walks up to the stage, you want to know if that ticket was actually sold, and where its stub sits in your list.
task: Write findTicket(tickets, drawn). tickets is sorted from smallest to largest and has no repeats. Return the index of drawn in tickets, or -1 if that number was never sold.
Use the sorted order: your solution should look at about log₂ n stubs, not all of them. An empty list returns -1.
constraints: tickets is strictly increasing (sorted, no repeats).

examples.explanation: Look at the middle stub first: index 3 holds 488. That is the drawn number, so the answer is 3 after a single look.

The middle stub is 488, which is less than 500, so 500 can only be to its right: 519, 760, 901. The middle of those is 760, too big, so look left of it: just 519. That is not 500 either, and nothing is left to check. Three looks, and 500 was never sold.

hints: Take the first example and look only at the middle stub, 488. If the drawn number were 700, which half of the list could you throw away without reading it?
One look at the middle rules out half of what is left, because the list is sorted. Keep the part that is still possible as a range from lo to hi.

Each round: look at the middle of the range. Equal means done. Too small means the answer is to the right, so move lo past the middle. Too big means move hi before it. When does the range become empty?
Start with lo = 0 and hi = n - 1. Loop while lo <= hi (the = matters: a range of one stub still needs checking). Set mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2) and compare. If the loop ends, return -1.
bruteForce: Read the stubs one by one from the start until you find the number or run out. That is correct and simple.

With 100,000 stubs it can take 100,000 looks for one call, and it ignores the most useful fact you have: the list is sorted. Binary search needs about 17 looks for the same list, because 2¹⁷ is more than 100,000.

py: def find_ticket(tickets: list[int], drawn: int) -> int:

tests.note: last ticket: catches loops that stop one step early

js: if (tickets[mid] < drawn) lo = mid + 1; // answer is to the right
else hi = mid - 1;                      // answer is to the left
return -1; // the range is empty: never sold
py: lo = mid + 1  # answer is to the right
hi = mid - 1  # answer is to the left
return -1  # the range is empty: never sold
walkthrough: A sorted list lets one comparison rule out half the candidates. Keep a range [lo, hi] of positions where the number could still be, and halve it each round.
• lo = 0, hi = 6, mid = 3. 488 < 500, so everything at index 3 or lower is too small. lo = 4.
• lo = 4, hi = 6, mid = 5. 760 > 500, so index 5 and above are too big. hi = 4.
• Now lo = 4 is past hi = 3. The range is empty, so return -1.

Notice step 3: the range held a single stub and still had to be checked. That is why the loop runs while lo <= hi, not lo < hi. With <, searching for 901 would stop before ever looking at the last stub.
Also notice the moves are mid + 1 and mid - 1, never just mid. You already checked mid, so leave it out. Keeping it can make the range stop shrinking and loop forever.
solution.timeWhy: Each round halves the range, so about log₂ n rounds.
solution.takeaway: In a sorted list, compare with the middle and throw away the half that cannot hold the answer. Keep an inclusive range lo..hi, loop while lo <= hi, and always move past mid. The other binary searches in this set change what you compare and which half you keep, but the halving is the same.
